name: The T Street Champion Linden

location.address: 3819 T St NW, Washington, DC (street tree, public sidewalk)

verified_sources: https://maps2.dcgis.dc.gov/dcgis/rest/services/DCGIS_DATA/Urban_Tree_Canopy/MapServer/23/query?where=OBJECTID=105903234&outFields=*&f=json (DDOT Urban Forestry Division tree inventory record FACILITYID 18456-380-3005-0216-000; condition: Excellent, assessed 2026-10-07; owner code: UFA (DDOT Urban Forestry Division street tree))

official_register.name: DDOT Urban Forestry Division public tree inventory (Open Data DC, CC BY 4.0)

access: Free. A street tree on a public sidewalk, viewable from the pavement at any hour.
transport: No Metro within about 1.5 km. Nearest is Foggy Bottom-GWU (about 2 km); Georgetown and Wisconsin Avenue buses are the usual approach.
story: Of all the lindens in Washington's care, the city's own arborists call this one the champion. The word sits in the District's street tree inventory, against a single sidewalk tree box at 3819 T Street NW, with no contest and no table of rivals behind it. Read it as a professional verdict rather than a prize, and as a single source, because the inventory is the only place it appears. The measurements back it up. The trunk is 55.4 inches across at chest height, about 4.4 metres round, and the crown, measured from the air by laser, rises about 73 feet and spreads over roughly 4,050 square feet of Burleith. That is a great deal of native basswood for one tree box on a residential street. The nearest thing to competition is a silver maple of 35 inches and a scatter of young trees. Its most recent inspection, on 7 October 2026, graded it Excellent. Getting here takes some intent. No Metro station lies within a kilometre and a half; Foggy Bottom-GWU is about two kilometres off, and the Georgetown and Wisconsin Avenue buses come closer. Nobody has dated it. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 55.4 inches across, far heavier than the silver maple and young trees near it. It stands in a sidewalk tree box in front of 3819 T Street NW.

name: The Hardy Park Elm

location.address: Hardy Park (DC Parks and Recreation), Foxhall / Palisades side of Georgetown, Washington, DC

verified_sources: https://maps2.dcgis.dc.gov/dcgis/rest/services/DCGIS_DATA/Urban_Tree_Canopy/MapServer/23/query?where=OBJECTID=106075713&outFields=*&f=json (DDOT Urban Forestry Division tree inventory record; condition: Good, assessed 2026-05-14 (pruned and injected against Dutch elm disease, 2025 and 2026 notes); owner code: DPR (DC Department of Parks and Recreation park tree))
https://opendata.dc.gov/datasets/urban-forestry-street-trees (DDOT Urban Forestry Division, CC BY 4.0)

official_register.name: DDOT Urban Forestry Division public tree inventory (Open Data DC, CC BY 4.0)

access: Free. A public DC park tree; open park hours.
transport: No Metro nearby; about 3 km from Foggy Bottom-GWU. Georgetown buses and a short ride from M Street.
story: Washington keeps a record of every tree on its public ground, and only one American elm in it comes close to this one. The trunk in Hardy Park measures 64.2 inches across at chest height, about five metres round, which puts it level with the elm on 38th Street NW as the two largest of their species the city's inventory lists on public land. What makes it look even bigger is the room it has had. Its crown covers about 6,600 square feet, roughly 615 square metres, the wide spreading shape of an elm that grew up in the open rather than squeezed between buildings. Beside it, the park's two Kwanzan cherries and a redbud look like seedlings. This one is kept alive on purpose. The record notes a pruning in March 2025 and an injection, the standard treatment against Dutch elm disease, and the tree was graded Good when an inspector last looked on 14 May 2026. All of this comes from one source, the city's tree inventory; the ground itself belongs to the Department of Parks and Recreation. Hardy Park sits on the Foxhall side of Georgetown, about three kilometres from Foggy Bottom-GWU Metro, so most people come by bus up from M Street. Nobody has written down how old it is. If you know, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the wide, open-grown crown, towering over two small Kwanzan cherries and a redbud. It stands in Hardy Park on the Foxhall side of Georgetown, the one big tree there.

name: The Volta Park Osage Orange

location.address: Volta Park, 1500 block of 34th St NW, Georgetown, Washington, DC

verified_sources: https://maps2.dcgis.dc.gov/dcgis/rest/services/DCGIS_DATA/Urban_Tree_Canopy/MapServer/23/query?where=OBJECTID=106069005&outFields=*&f=json (DDOT Urban Forestry Division tree inventory record FACILITYID 10340-155-3001-0095-000; condition: Fair, assessed 2026-08-19 (lost a 4 in branch in the January 2025 snow storm); owner code: DPR (DC Department of Parks and Recreation park tree))

official_register.name: DDOT Urban Forestry Division public tree inventory (Open Data DC, CC BY 4.0)

access: Free. A public DC park (Volta Park); open park hours.
transport: Foggy Bottom-GWU Metro about 2 km; Georgetown buses; walkable from Dumbarton Oaks Park and Montrose Park (about 1 km) so it joins the Georgetown cluster (wdc_011, wdc_014, wdc_018).
story: Washington's tree inventory knows of no bigger Osage orange than this one in Volta Park, and the margin is wide. Its trunk measures 57.2 inches across at chest height, about 4.6 metres round. The Osage oranges growing around it in the same park run from 19.6 to 38.1 inches, so this is not a lone giant but the head of a small family, and the group itself is worth a look. Take the big number with one honest caveat. Osage orange rarely reaches a trunk this size, and the record does not say whether the city's arborist measured one stem or several grown together, so it may be a multi-stemmed tree read as one. Either way it is the biggest trunk of its kind the District has on file. The crown is modest by comparison, about 63 feet high and 950 square feet across. The inventory records a four-inch branch lost in the snow storm of January 2025, and the last inspection, in August 2026, graded it Fair rather than Good. Volta Park is a neighbourhood park in the middle of Georgetown, a short walk from Dumbarton Oaks Park and Montrose Park, about a kilometre away, which makes it an easy addition to a Georgetown walk. Foggy Bottom-GWU Metro is about two kilometres off. Nobody has dated it. If you know when these trees went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the largest of the Osage oranges in Volta Park, its trunk 57.2 inches across where the others are 20 to 38. It stands in Volta Park off 34th Street NW, Georgetown.

location.address: Park opposite 6112 Banks Pl NE (6201 Banks Pl NE in the inventory), Washington, DC

verified_sources: https://maps2.dcgis.dc.gov/dcgis/rest/services/DCGIS_DATA/Urban_Tree_Canopy/MapServer/23/query?where=OBJECTID=106070398&outFields=*&f=json (DDOT Urban Forestry Division tree inventory record; condition: Good, assessed 2025-07-24 (deadwood and clearance prune); owner code: DPR (DC Department of Parks and Recreation park tree))
https://opendata.dc.gov/datasets/urban-forestry-street-trees (DDOT Urban Forestry Division, CC BY 4.0)

official_register.name: DDOT Urban Forestry Division public tree inventory (Open Data DC, CC BY 4.0)

access: Free. A public DC park tree beside Banks Place NE.
transport: Benning Road Metro about 2 km; Minnesota Avenue Metro about 3 km. Not walkable from the Mall cluster.
story: No willow oak on a Washington city park is recorded bigger than this one, and it stands in a small green on Banks Place NE, far from the Mall and almost entirely alone. The District's tree inventory puts its trunk at 67.4 inches across, about 5.4 metres round, more than any other willow oak on Parks and Recreation ground in the city's list. Laser measurements from the air give it a crown about 88 feet high and roughly 5,670 square feet wide, the broad shape of a tree with nothing crowding it. Everything else within twenty metres is a sapling, newly planted honeylocusts, horse chestnuts and a hackberry with trunks one or two inches thick, so the park looks like a nursery gathered around a single grown-up. A second willow oak, 53.6 inches across, stands about 200 metres east, opposite 6220 Banks Place. Do not mistake size for great age here. Casey Trees, whose 2023 big-tree contest found willow oaks up to 83 inches across in DC, calls them fast growers, so this one is very likely well under 150 years old, and nobody has a planting date. When the city last checked it, in July 2025, it took out some deadwood and graded the tree Good. One source, the city's inventory, stands behind all of this. The nearest Metro is Benning Road, about two kilometres away. If you know when it went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the only big tree in the park, a willow oak 67.4 inches across surrounded by newly planted saplings. It stands in the small park opposite 6112 Banks Place NE.

access: Free. A street tree on a public sidewalk.
transport: Columbia Heights Metro about 0.7 km (roughly 9 minutes on foot).
story: Four oaks stand within twenty metres of each other on this stretch of Harvard Street NW, and one of them is nearly twice as thick as the other three. The city's tree inventory gives the two pin oaks 31 and 34 inches across and a second willow oak 32.5. This one measures 61.5 inches, about 4.9 metres round, in a sidewalk tree box in front of number 1661. Look up and the gap widens. Laser surveys from the air put its crown at about 90 feet high and roughly 5,100 square feet across, a canopy of park size over a city sidewalk on the edge of Mount Pleasant and Columbia Heights. The neighbours are not small trees either, which is what makes the comparison so lopsided. When the city's arborists last inspected this one, in June 2025, they noted some deadwood and still graded it Excellent. That record is the single source for everything here; nobody else has measured it or written it up. It is an easy one to reach. Columbia Heights Metro is about 700 metres away, roughly nine minutes on foot, and the tree is on the public pavement at any hour. Nobody has dated it. If you know when this stretch of Harvard Street was planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 61.5 inches across, nearly twice the girth of the pin oaks and the smaller willow oak beside it. It stands in front of 1661 Harvard Street NW.
